There is a peculiar comfort in the hour before dawn. The world has not yet made its demands. Roads lie empty, windows remain dark, and even familiar places seem briefly unclaimed.

In that hour, a person can imagine that life is less like a straight road and more like a house filled with doors. Some were opened by choice. Others swung inward because of luck, grief, curiosity, or someone else’s hand. A few remain locked, and we spend years wondering what might be behind them.

But perhaps a good life is not the one in which every door is opened. Perhaps it is enough to enter a few rooms fully—to notice the dust turning gold in the sunlight, to learn where the floorboards creak, to sit with the people who arrive there, and to leave something kind behind when it is time to go.

Soon morning comes. A kettle clicks off. A bus exhales at the curb. Somewhere, a tired baker lifts warm bread from an oven. The ordinary world resumes, carrying within it all the mystery it had before dawn—only now disguised as errands, conversations, and cups of coffee.

Most miracles are like that. They do not announce themselves. They wait to be noticed.
